organizations.canonical_name: Independent Grenadier Company, Polish Armed Forces in the West
organizations.historical_name: Samodzielna Kompania Grenadierów Polskich Sił Zbrojnych
organizations.normalization_notes: A Polish Armed Forces in the West unit administered the Project Eagle volunteers while they trained and served with OSS. It is modeled as a military assignment, never as civilian employment.

affiliations.organization_name_as_found: Samodzielna Kompania Grenadierów Polskich Sił Zbrojnych
affiliations.role_title: Sergeant and Project Eagle radio operator
affiliations.date_precision: Micgiel documents that Project Eagle volunteers came from the Independent Grenadier Company, remained under Polish military authority and company administration during the project, and returned to the Polish Army on 31 May 1945. Edmund Barski is identified as the Manhattan mission radio operator.
affiliations.research_notes: This is the military pathway through which Barski entered and remained administratively attached during Project Eagle. It is not a civilian employer. His last civilian employer remains unidentified; a forced labor assignment and German conscription are not converted into voluntary employment.

claims.claim_text: The indexed Edmund Barski is high-confidence matched to the Polish Project Eagle radio operator also documented through the Zeitz or Zeic family name.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: Micgiel's archive-based monograph identifies Edmund Barski as the 21-year-old radio operator in the Manhattan mission and cites his OSS personnel and mission files.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High confidence from the uncommon exact name, the index's Polish Army note and sergeant context, and the monograph's explicit OSS Project Eagle role and NARA file citations.
claims.temporal_assessment: The monograph places Barski in the Polish military Project Eagle cohort from selection and training in 1944 through the April 1945 Manhattan mission.
claims.match_notes: The match remains high confidence rather than confirmed until Box 40 is directly compared with the cited Project Eagle personnel file. The similarly named Polish officer Eugeniusz Borowski, who used Edmund Barski as an alias, was rejected as a different person.

claims.claim_text: Edmund Barski's immediate military pathway into Project Eagle was the Independent Grenadier Company of the Polish Armed Forces in the West.
claims.evidence_excerpt: ochotnicy z Samodzielnej Kompanii Grenadierów PSZ
claims.evidence_paraphrase: Micgiel states that Project Eagle volunteers came from the Independent Grenadier Company and remained under Polish military authority and company administration while assigned to OSS.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High-confidence identity from the exact uncommon name, Polish Army note, sergeant context, and explicit Project Eagle radio-operator biography.
claims.temporal_assessment: Explicit immediate pathway. The cohort was selected from the company, remained administratively attached during OSS service, and returned to the Polish Army on 31 May 1945.
claims.match_notes: Displayed as a military assignment and excluded from civilian-employer counts. No named civilian employer is supported by the reviewed evidence.

claims.claim_text: The indexed Paul F. Bartasavich is high-confidence matched to the Paul F. Bartasavich listed in the 10th Mountain Division's 86th Infantry.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: Denver Public Library's institutional 10th Mountain Division index records the same rare full name and middle initial in Company B, 86th Infantry.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High confidence from the exact, highly distinctive full name and middle initial in two wartime military contexts. The institutional roster does not itself mention OSS.
claims.temporal_assessment: The roster establishes World War II Army service but does not establish whether the 86th Infantry assignment preceded, overlapped, or followed OSS-related service.
claims.match_notes: No affiliation claim is published because the temporal relation between the 86th Infantry and OSS is unresolved. RA1303 remains unexpanded as printed in the index.

claims.claim_text: The indexed French S/Lt Jean Barthelemy is high-confidence matched to the Jean Barthelemy who served on the OSS/Sussex Velours mission under the variants Jean Berthet and Jean Berton.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Sussex/Ossex/OSS Velours (Jean Barthelemy @Jean Berthet @Jean Berton badge n°98
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The mission chronology names Jean Barthelemy and two variants on the OSS/Sussex Velours mission and points to NARA and French defense files; the SHD index lists his individual dossier.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High confidence from the exact name, French military context in the index, explicit OSS mission association, named operational aliases, badge reference, and a matching French archival dossier pointer.
claims.temporal_assessment: The Velours chronology dates the mission insertion to 1 September 1944. It does not identify Barthelemy's last employer or the precise pre-OSS French assignment.
claims.match_notes: The identity remains high confidence rather than confirmed until Box 40 and the French dossier are reviewed together. A different Free French artillery namesake with a separate dossier number and grade history was rejected.
